title: These Two Planets Are Fluffier Than Cotton Candy!
summary:
Imagine a planet so light and fluffy that it could float in a giant bathtub. Astronomers just found two of them! They're called TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, and they're less dense than cotton candy. That means if you could put one in a huge pool of water, it might float like a beach ball.

These planets are called "super-puffs." They're the size of Jupiter, the biggest planet in our solar system, but they're incredibly light. They orbit a star like our Sun, about 1,113 light-years away. That's super far — a light-year is how far light travels in a whole year!

How did scientists find them? Volunteers were looking at pictures from a NASA space telescope called TESS. They noticed tiny dips in a star's brightness. Those dips meant planets were passing in front of the star, blocking a bit of its light.

Scientists used telescopes all over the world to check. One telescope in Antarctica was extra helpful because it stays dark all winter. It watched the planets cross the star for more than 11 hours — the longest ever seen from the ground!

Scientists still don't know how these fluffy planets form. Maybe they have big puffy clouds of gas around tiny rocky centers. The team hopes a bigger telescope called James Webb will solve the mystery.
why_it_matters: This shows that space can be stranger than anything you can imagine, and that even ordinary volunteers looking at pictures can help scientists make a real discovery.

background_read: Scientists have found a few other 'super-puff' planets before, but they are very rare, so every new one is exciting.
NASA (the U.S. space agency) runs TESS, a telescope in space that has been searching the sky for planets since 2018.
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, is the largest space telescope ever built and can study the air around faraway planets.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers and volunteers who studied pictures from NASA's TESS space telescope
WHAT: They found two 'super-puff' planets, TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, that are less dense than cotton candy
WHERE: About 1,113 light-years away, orbiting a star like our Sun — checked by telescopes around the world, including one in Antarctica
WHY: The planets are so light that no one knows how they form, and the James Webb telescope may solve the mystery

perspectives.description: These planets are a wonderful mystery, and the James Webb telescope could finally explain how such light, fluffy worlds are made.
We can only guess for now — maybe these planets have puffy clouds of gas around tiny rocky centers, but we need more data to be sure.
This proves that anyone — even volunteers checking photos — can be part of a real space discovery, not just grown-up experts.
